ExplanationParts.CorpusEarnedOpening: In Baizhang's wild-fox case, 'not falling into cause and effect' is the old man's fatal answer; later speakers repeatedly raise and question it against 'not obscuring cause and effect.'
EvidenceBody: An old man who remained after Baizhang's addresses says that in the time of Kāśyapa Buddha he had lived on that mountain. A student asked him, “does a person of great conduct still fall into cause and effect or not?” He answered, “does not fall into cause and effect” (大修行底人還落因果也無？不落因果). The record says this answer was followed by five hundred lives in a wild-fox body. The old man asks Baizhang to give a substitute turning phrase; Baizhang answers, “does not obscure cause and effect” (不昧因果), and the old man awakens at the words. The record continues with the old man's request for a deceased monk's funeral and Huangbo's later question to Baizhang about the case. Wumen asks directly, “Not falling into cause and effect—why did he fall into a wild fox? Not obscuring cause and effect—why was he released from the wild fox?” (不落因果，為甚墮野狐？不昧因果，為甚脫野狐？). Wansong retells the same speaker turns in his commentary. A later master questions a student on the stated difference between falling and not obscuring, while an earlier lamp dialogue rebukes the cited participant's “then it does not fall into cause and effect” with “do not make a wild-jackal cry” (莫作野干鳴). The exact phrase occurs 151 times in 82 allowlisted files.

A later record preserves two unnamed monks disputing the case: one says that 'not obscuring' still did not shed the fox body, while the other asks how 'not falling' ever incurred it. Chaozong's record also has an unnamed monk publicly ask why 'not falling into cause and effect' led to the fox. These are distinct later interrogations of the same case phrase, not new senses.
